extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of 17th-century British/Scottish political history
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length historical narrative about James Graham, Marquis of Montrose, his politics and actions during the Bishops' Wars and the Covenanting period, with embedded normative statements about governance, military law, and political conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between Crown and Nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: "the Crown and the nobility should mutually support and counterpoise each other, both acting together against the dangerous encroachments of the people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a principle of good constitutional order in the author's ideal State; contrasted with other views (e.g., Argyll's) that anticipated the rise of the middle classes and demanded different checks. Implies mutual support/checking roles rather than dominance by one estate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament should represent the people rather than the sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: "Henceforth the Scottish Parliament, like the English Parliament, must represent the voice, not of the sovereign, but of the people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify constitutional reforms and the curbing of royal influence; linked with procedural changes (Estates choosing their own Lords) that effectively silence the sovereign's direct voice in Parliament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each Estate elects its own Lords / numerical voting reform
rubrics_metrics.description: "By a majority of only one it was determined that in future each Estate should choose its own Lords. Henceforth the nobles would be represented by eight votes, the lesser barons and burghers by sixteen; and thus at one stroke the voice of the sovereign was silenced in the Scottish Parliament."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific institutional reform: allocation of votes among Estates as a mechanism to shift balance of power toward non-sovereign representation; presented as decisive and comparable to major reform bills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair taxation across factions to cover war expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: "A general tax was to be levied, to cover the expenses of the late war, on Royalists as well as on Covenanters."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle of impartial fiscal burden in post-conflict settlement; presented as part of measures that constrained royal influence and asserted parliamentary authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garrison appointments should be national and subject to parliamentary approval
rubrics_metrics.description: "The castles of Edinburgh, Stirling, and Dumbarton were to be entrusted to the charge of none but Scottish subjects, who, though chosen by the King, were to be approved by Parliament."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines a nationality requirement for key defenses with parliamentary oversight of royal nominations; an example of limiting royal prerogative via parliamentary checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of secret correspondence with the enemy (military discipline)
rubrics_metrics.description: "a general order had been issued by Leslie that no communication should be held with the enemy except under his warrant. Anything in the nature of a secret correspondence was declared treasonable, and he who held it liable to the punishment of a traitor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military-legal standard codified in articles of war; used to charge Montrose when a letter to the King was discovered. Illustrates how secret communications were treated as a capital offence in the army's regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treason defined broadly in articles of war (speech against the King)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the same articles declare that, 'If any man shall open his mouth against the King's majesty's person or authority, or shall presume to touch his sacred person, he shall be punished as a traitor'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows the legalistic scope of treason under army regulations—covering spoken opposition as well as acts—creating a strict standard for loyalty and discipline within the Covenanting forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misuse of commissions (anti-pattern: commissions as cover for private vengeance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissions of 'fire and sword' were issued for pacification, but commanders (e.g., Argyll, Monro) sometimes used them to harry, destroy property, torture citizens, and settle private feuds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning/example that broad wartime commissions can be abused to perpetrate private vengeance; the narrative treats such behaviour as brutal and illegitimate, contrasting official purpose with practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointments to high office should be made for ability and honesty (avoid patronage)
rubrics_metrics.description: "settle the high offices of State upon men chosen by himself according to his own knowledge of their ability and honesty. Men who owe their preferment to the recommendation of others will not serve him well if it must be to the prejudice of their patrons."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice directed to the sovereign: prefer merit and integrity over recommendations or factional patronage; warns that patronage undermines effective governance and loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice temperate government; avoid absolutism and flatterers
rubrics_metrics.description: "He is bid to beware of Rehoboam's counsellors: 'they are flatterers, and therefore cannot be friends; they follow your fortune and love not your person.' ... not to aim at absoluteness, which of all people the Scots will least endure. 'Practice, sir, the temperate government.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance on style of rule: temperance (moderation) secures durable authority and popular goodwill; absolutism and sycophancy are political dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign must retain sufficient power to punish oppression and maintain peace and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: "A king's authority should be maintained to the height allowed by the law of God and Nature, and the fundamental laws of the country. If not it sinks into contempt; and 'weak and miserable is that people whose prince hath not power sufficient to punish oppression, and to maintain peace and justice.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balances the previous cautions: while warning against absolutism, the text insists on the necessity of adequate sovereign authority for law, justice, and stability; presented as a condition for a healthy polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal consequences for false testimony and 'leasing-making' (perjury/defamation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An accused witness (Ladywell) was tried and executed 'under that old statute of leasing-making' after confessing and recanting; the statute punished creating and spreading falsehoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows the period's legal instrument for punishing false accusations or slander; narrative notes how confessions under pressure and subsequent recantations complicate assessments of truth and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion in political speech; danger of loose talk and leaking plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Montrose's habit of talking freely about plots, the Bond and the Dictatorship to many people led to the exposure of the secret alliance and contributed to his downfall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An implicit conduct standard: political actors must exercise restraint in speech and in whom they confide; loose talk is depicted as an anti-pattern that risks discovery, imprisonment, or worse.
